newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Foreign observers arrive for Chechen elections.
newsitem.headline: Foreign observers arrive for Chechen elections.

text.p: Several dozen foreign observers flew in to Chechnya on Saturday to monitor presidential and parliamentary elections to be held in the breakaway Russian region on Monday.

Several members of the group, which will total 75 under the auspices of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said they had no worries for their safety, despite recent attacks on foreigners and warnings from Chechen leaders that there could be more trouble around the poll.
"I see no reason to worry. I know Chechnya," Danish diplomat Peter Christensen told Reuters at Grozny airport.
"I think the security arrangements are very, very well thought through," a Swedish colleague added. "I don't think there is very much risk."
Chechen authorities have stepped up security since the killing of six foreign Red Cross workers last month, which local officials blamed on Russian security forces.

The murders of several ethnic Russians and the separate kidnappings of two Russian priests and two Russian television journalists have heightened fears of "provocations". The priests were released unharmed on Friday.

OSCE officials have said the observers from 12 member states, who will be joined by 40 or so independent monitors from countries including Russia, will be provided with armed escorts by the Chechen separatist administration.

The OSCE, which helped mediate last year's peace that saw the separatists establish de facto independence and Russian troops leave the region, is donating some $600,000 to Chechnya to organise the election. Some Moscow politicians have accused the agency of breaking Russian laws on election financing.
Sixteen candidates are running for the post of president.

The OSCE observers were guarded in their comments on the fairness of the election. Senior figures in the organisation have said that the monitors will not be making their views public until after the voting and counting is over.
"We're here to see there are free and fair elections," Christensen said. Like his colleagues, when asked if he expected that to be the case he replied simply: "We'll see."
Russian Security Council secretary Ivan Rybkin, whose predecessor Alexander Lebed negotiated the peace, also flew in to Grozny on Saturday for talks with local officials.
